doc.title: Configuration
doc.paragraph: An Adaptive Framework application is configured by a configuration file, usually named afw.conf, and optionally by service configuration objects kept in a configuration adapter. This chapter describes the file, each type of entry it can hold, and how services are configured and started.

section.title: The Configuration File
section.paragraph: Both afw and afwfcgi read the configuration file named by their -f option. afwfcgi reads afw.conf in its working directory when -f is not given; afw without -f runs with only core functionality.

The file holds an array of configuration entries. Each entry is an object whose type property says what it configures. Entries are processed in order, so an entry can use anything an earlier entry set up. By default the file is parsed as relaxed JSON: standard JSON plus block comments (/* ... */), line comments (//), unquoted property names and trailing commas. Use the -t option to read it in another content type, such as yaml; the extension that provides it is loaded on demand (see Extensions below).

Every entry also accepts the common properties below. The sourceLocation property is added by Adaptive Framework, as the file path and entry number, and is used in error messages, so an error names the entry that caused it.
The configuration types available are:

row.column: An adapter: a store of objects, chosen by adapterType.
The application itself. There is at most one application entry.
A handler that makes authorization decisions, chosen by authorizationHandlerType.
A destination for log messages, chosen by logType.
How requests under a URI prefix are processed, chosen by requestHandlerType.

section.paragraph: Configuration errors, such as a missing required property, are logged one per line with the entry and property they concern (for example afw.conf entry 1.env.mode> value required), and the application does not start.

section.title: Application
section.paragraph: The application entry names the application and sets application-wide behavior: the configuration adapter, the extensions to load at startup, authorization control, qualified variables available to every script, file paths, and limits. At run time this entry can be read as the object /afw/_AdaptiveApplication_/current.

When the application has a confAdapterId, the object _AdaptiveConf_application/<applicationId> in that adapter, if there is one, adds properties to the entry. For the file adapter in the example above, that is /var/lib/afw/config/_AdaptiveConf_application/MyApplication.json. A property set in the configuration file wins, and a different value for it in the object is logged as a warning.

Variables in qualifiedVariables are available to every script and template under their qualifier. For example, qualifiedVariables: { app: { supportEmail: "help@example.com" } } makes app::supportEmail available. Values may be expressions or templates that are evaluated when they are read.

rootFilePaths maps a path prefix to a host directory, such as rootFilePaths: { data: "/var/lib/afw/data/" }. Script file functions (open_file, compile_from_file, eval_from_file) take a path such as data/report.txt, which resolves under the directory of the longest matching prefix. A path that matches no prefix, contains .., or leaves its root is refused.

The limit*, *ChunkMin, memoryRegion* and threadStackBytes properties override built-in defaults that suit most applications. Change them when a measurement calls for it, for example raising limitRequestPoolBytes when large requests fail with payload_too_large.

section.title: Adapters
section.paragraph: An adapter entry creates an adapter, identified by its adapterId, of the type named by adapterType. The properties every adapter accepts are below; each adapter type adds its own, described in the chapter.
The adapter afw always exists. It is provided by core and holds the runtime objects: object types, functions, data types, services and the rest of the running configuration.

section.title: Extensions
section.paragraph: An extension is a shared library that registers more adapter types, log types, content types, functions or data types. An extension shipped with Adaptive Framework is usually loaded on demand: the first time a configuration entry or script uses something the extension registers, such as adapterType: "lmdb", core finds the extension that provides it in its manifest and loads it. An extension entry, the application's extensions property, or the -e option of afw and afwfcgi loads one explicitly, which is needed for an extension that is not in a manifest.

section.title: Logs
section.paragraph: A log entry sends log messages to a destination. The standard log type writes to standard output; syslog (Linux) and event_log (Windows) write to the system log. Each priority property, such as info or debug, includes the messages of that priority; filter and format are scripts and templates that select and shape messages.
A log is a service named log- followed by its logId. This entry writes messages of priority info and more severe to standard output:
section.code: { type : "log", logId : "console", logType : "standard", err : true, warning : true, notice : true, info : true }
section.paragraph: The syslog log type accepts the properties below, but at present it always logs with facility daemon and the process name, whatever ident, facility and the option* properties say.

section.title: Request Handlers
section.paragraph: A requestHandler entry decides how afwfcgi processes the requests whose URI begins with uriPrefix. The request handler type provided by core is adapter, which serves the objects of the configured adapters over HTTP (see the Web Services chapter of the Developer Guide). Requests for POST /afw actions, used by the Administrative Web App and language bindings, are served by the same handler.

section.title: Authorization Handlers
section.paragraph:
An authorizationHandler entry adds a handler that takes part in authorization decisions. Its properties, and the application's authorizationControl, are described in the
chapter.

section.title: Services
section.paragraph: Adapters, logs and authorization handlers run as services, which have a status and can be started, stopped and restarted while the application runs. Each service has an id made of its configuration type and id joined with a dash: the adapter lmdb is the service adapter-lmdb. Services are listed as _AdaptiveService_ objects in the afw adapter, and the Administrative Web App manages them under Admin, Services.
Services can be defined in two places:

list.item: An entry in the configuration file is a permanent service. It starts with the application and cannot be stopped or changed without restarting the application.

An _AdaptiveServiceConf_ object in the adapter named by the application's confAdapterId is a service that can be changed, stopped, started and restarted at run time. Its conf property holds the same entry that would be written in the configuration file.

section.paragraph: The values of startup are:

row.column: Started when the application starts; can be stopped and started by hand.
Started and stopped by hand only. This is the default.
Reported for services defined in the configuration file. Not allowed in an _AdaptiveServiceConf_ object.
